WHERE enabled AND next_run_at <= $1` with no `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, no claim column and no transaction spanning the read and the `Record` write, so every worker process selects the same due rows and runs them concurrently — R5 (read then separate write, TOCTOU) and R49 (docs/scheduled-exports.md asserts single-claim semantics as an enforceable property).

title: 500 000-row LIMIT truncates silently, on a non-total order
what_is_wrong: A window with more than `maxRows` rows is cut with no signal of any kind, and the cut is made on `occurred_at` alone — a wall-clock value with no uniqueness or total order, so which rows land on either side of the boundary is undefined among same-instant records (R57).

title: 500,000-row truncation is silent and the ordering key has no total order
what_is_wrong: a window with more than `maxRows` rows is cut without any signal — `serialize` returns `n` and the run is recorded `succeeded` — and because `occurred_at` is a wall-clock timestamp with ties, which rows fall on the losing side of the cut is undefined.

title: 500k-row cap truncates the export silently and the missing rows are never re-exported
what_is_wrong: the query caps at `maxRows` with no detection of having hit the cap, so a busy org's window is cut off at exactly 500000 rows and the run still reports `succeeded`; because the next window starts after this one ends, the discarded rows are never exported by any later run.

title: A window larger than maxRows is silently truncated and reported as a success
what_is_wrong: The query caps the result at 500,000 rows with no signal, so an oversized window produces a short file that `runSchedule` records as `succeeded`; worse, `occurred_at` is not a total order, so which rows survive the cut among same-instant records is undefined.

title: AddDate across a DST transition can shift the local hour
what_is_wrong: `AddDate` normalises a wall-clock time that does not exist in the target zone (the spring-forward gap), so a schedule set to an hour inside the gap fires an hour off on that day.

title: CSV and JSONL do not carry the same values for the same row
what_is_wrong: the CSV branch routes every value through `formatValue`, which stringifies `[]byte` and normalises `time.Time` to `t.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)`, while the JSONL branch hands the raw driver value to `encoding/json` — which base64-encodes `[]byte` (the shape most Postgres text and bytea columns scan into through `any`) and marshals `time.Time` in its original offset — so docs/scheduled-exports.md's promise that JSONL carries "those same keys and the same values" and that "Timestamps are RFC 3339 in UTC" is false for the JSONL format. title: `serialize`, `Store`, and `Worker` ship with no test at all

title: a cancelled context leaves the schedule unadvanced

title: a daily hour that does not exist on a DST spring-forward day shifts silently
what_is_wrong: On the spring-forward date `time.Date` normalizes a non-existent local hour (`hour_of_day = 2` in `Europe/Berlin`, say) to the adjacent real instant, so that day's run happens an hour off the configured time with no record of the substitution.

title: a daily schedule set to a non-existent local hour fires an hour early on the DST spring-forward day
what_is_wrong: `time.Date` normalizes a wall-clock time that the location skips — executed for `America/New_York`, `hour_of_day = 2` on 2024-03-10 yields 01:00 EST (06:00 UTC), an hour before the intended slot.

title: a daily schedule whose hour falls in a DST spring-forward gap fires an hour late
what_is_wrong: `time.Date` normalizes a wall-clock time that does not exist in `loc` (e.g. 02:00 in `Europe/Berlin` on the spring-forward Sunday) to the following instant, so that day's run happens at 03:00 local.

title: a due schedule is not claimed — it re-runs every 30s until `Record` succeeds, and concurrent workers duplicate it
what_is_wrong: `Due` is a plain `SELECT … WHERE enabled AND next_run_at <= $1` with no lock, no claim column and no `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and `next_run_at` is only advanced by `Record` *after* the upload finishes — so nothing makes a run at-most-once, and when `Record` fails the code merely logs `"could not advance schedule"` and leaves the row due. `docs/scheduled-exports.md` claims the opposite: "a schedule is claimed by one worker, so a due run happens once even with several workers live" (R49; R5, a read followed by an unguarded write).

title: a failed Record leaves the schedule due forever, re-exporting every 30 seconds
what_is_wrong: when `Record` fails the error is logged and nothing else happens, so `next_run_at` still holds a past instant and the very next poll selects the same schedule again.

what_is_wrong: the window is a fixed duration subtracted from the moment the worker happened to pick the schedule up, not the interval since the previous run's end, so any difference between the scheduled instant and the actual start — up to a full 30-second poll interval, longer under backlog, and exactly one hour on each DST transition for a daily schedule in a zone like `Europe/Berlin` — becomes either a gap or an overlap.

title: the export window is measured from wall-clock now, so runs do not tile and a late or missed run drops rows permanently
what_is_wrong: The window's end is the instant the worker happened to execute, not the schedule's slot, while `NextRun(s, startedAt)` advances to the exact slot boundary — so consecutive runs are separated by `24h + (δ₂ − δ₁)` where δ is the per-run poll/queue delay, leaving a gap of `δ₂ − δ₁` when the delay grows and a duplicate overlap when it shrinks, and a worker outage of any length still yields exactly one `window(cadence)` slice on restart. This contradicts the doc's "consecutive objects tile the timeline ... no gaps and no duplicated rows".

title: the first run of a new schedule exports data from before the schedule existed
what_is_wrong: the first run has no predecessor, so its window reaches a full cadence back past the schedule's creation, contradicting "A run covers exactly the interval since the run before it".
